name: Design an Offline-First Sync Engine
intent: Let an app read and change its data with no connection, then merge every device's changes into one consistent set of records when the connection returns, without losing edits, duplicating them or resurrecting deleted rows.
codeTitle: a sync engine with an outbox, per-field merge and tombstones
finalIntro: A technician edits a work order in a basement with no signal, and the change reaches the manager's tablet later.
prompt: Design the data layer of a field-service app used by 300,000 technicians and managers, on phones and tablets. They open work orders, fill in checklists, change a stock count and attach photos and videos, often with no signal. The app must work fully offline, merge changes from several devices when they reconnect, and still cope with a phone that comes back after a month.
functional: Read and edit work orders, checklists and parts counts with no connection
Send local changes to the server and receive other people's changes when online
Merge edits made on different devices to the same record
Delete records so that the deletion reaches every device
Show each person only the work orders they are allowed to see
Upload large photos and videos, and resume after a dropped connection
Update the app and its local database without losing unsent changes
nonFunctional: Every screen reads from the device and responds in under 50 ms, online or not
Never lose an edit that the user saw succeed, and never apply one twice
A change reaches another online device within a few seconds
Handle about 10 million edits per day, about 400 per second in the busiest hour
A phone that was offline for 30 days must catch up correctly without manual repair
A device with a wrong clock must not be able to overwrite newer work
A user who loses access to a project stops receiving its data

firstAttempt.text: A normal client and server. The app calls the REST API for every screen and saves a whole work order with a PUT when the user taps save. A cache of recent responses is kept for a bad connection, and the newest save wins.
limits: With no signal the app shows spinners and errors, and an edit made in a basement is lost or blocked
A save that times out may or may not have reached the server, so retrying it can duplicate a change or overwrite a newer one
Saving the whole record means the last save wins, and one technician's checklist overwrites the manager's change to the priority
Every app launch downloads everything again, because the client has no way to ask only for what changed
Deleted work orders stay on devices that missed the delete, or come back when an old device saves them
Each user is sent data for work orders they have no right to see

steps.title: Make the local database the source of truth for the screen
steps.problem: A screen that waits for the network is slow on a good connection and useless on a bad one. A technician in a basement cannot open the checklist they were about to fill in.
steps.fix: Put a real database on the device, such as SQLite, or IndexedDB in a browser. The user interface only ever reads from it and writes to it, usually through queries that re-run when the data changes, so a screen answers in a few milliseconds whether or not there is a signal. The network is a background job that copies data in both directions. The local schema has a version number, and migrations run once at start-up inside a transaction, in small steps, before any screen reads.
steps.tradeoff: The app is instant and works anywhere. Each device now holds a replica that can be stale, corrupted or on an old schema, so the server has to treat every client as an unreliable copy, and the app has the extra work of local migrations and storage limits.

steps.title: Record every change in an outbox with an idempotent id
steps.problem: A save that times out may or may not have reached the server. Retrying could apply it twice, and not retrying could lose it, and a phone can be closed or killed at any time between the two.
steps.fix: Each local write inserts an outbox row in the same local transaction as the data change. The row holds a mutation id made of the device id and a counter (or a UUID), the record, the field or operation, the new value and the client timestamp. A sync loop sends the rows in order in batches, with retries using exponential backoff and jitter. The server keeps the ids it has applied, which can be a single highest counter per device, and acknowledges a repeated mutation without applying it again. Mutations to the same field that are still unsent can be collapsed into one.
steps.tradeoff: A change the user saw succeed is never lost and never applied twice, even if the app dies halfway. The server must remember ids for as long as a client may retry, and the outbox can grow large during a long offline period unless it is collapsed.

steps.title: Pull changes incrementally with a cursor per collection
steps.problem: Downloading everything on every launch wastes battery and data, and asking for rows changed since a timestamp misses changes, because a transaction with an earlier timestamp can commit after a later one.
steps.fix: The server appends every accepted change to a change log and gives it a sequence number from a counter, so entries become visible in a single order. The client keeps one cursor per collection (work orders, checklists, parts) and asks for the changes after its cursor, up to a page size such as 500, and the reply carries the next cursor and whether more remain. The client applies the page and moves the cursor in one local transaction, so a crash in the middle just repeats a page. A push notification or open connection only hints that something changed, and the client then pulls.
steps.tradeoff: A device that was online a minute ago downloads a few hundred bytes. The server must keep a log and the sequence has to be cheap to produce and read in order, and the log has to be kept as long as devices may return.

steps.title: Merge conflicts field by field, and ask only when it matters
steps.problem: Two people edit the same work order on two phones while offline. If the whole record is replaced by the newest save, the checklist saved at 14:05 wipes out the priority the manager set at 14:03, and a phone with a clock 20 minutes fast beats everyone.
steps.fix: Store each field with its own timestamp and device id, and merge field by field, so edits to different fields all survive. Use a hybrid logical clock: a new timestamp is the larger of the wall clock and one more than anything the device has seen, so an edit made after seeing a change always sorts after it, whatever the wall clock says. For values that can be added to, store the change rather than the result: a counter holds increments per device and a set holds adds and removes, so two people taking parts from stock both count. Keep both versions of a long note or a signed form and put them in a review queue for a person to choose.
steps.tradeoff: Almost every concurrent edit merges without anybody noticing, and a clock error cannot undo informed work. Each field carries about 20 bytes of metadata, special types limit the data model, and when two people change the same plain field blind, one of the edits is dropped unless the app asks.

steps.title: Delete with tombstones, collect them, and reset devices that were away too long
steps.problem: If a delete simply removes the row, a phone that was offline still has it and sends it back, so deleted work orders come back from the dead. Keeping every tombstone for ever makes the log and the tables grow without limit.
steps.fix: A delete is a write like any other: the record is marked gone with a timestamp, and the mark is replicated to every device. The server keeps tombstones for longer than the longest time a device may be away, for example 35 days for a 30-day promise, then removes them and records a floor, the highest sequence number it has forgotten. A client whose cursor is below the floor is told to reset: it first pushes its outbox, then throws away its replica and downloads a fresh snapshot, which also removes rows that were deleted while it was away. Mutations older than the floor on collected records are sent to the review queue instead of recreating them.
steps.tradeoff: Storage stays bounded and old phones always converge. A phone back after 31 days pays for a full download, for example 0.6 MB compressed, and the offline limit is a product rule that users sometimes hit.

steps.title: Sync only what the user may see, and upload big files on the side
steps.problem: Sending a technician every work order in the company is slow, fills the phone and leaks data. A 200 MB video also cannot travel inside a mutation, because a dropped connection at 90% would start the upload again.
steps.fix: Every change in the log is tagged with the project or team it belongs to, and the access filter keeps only the changes that the user may see when pulling. When access is granted the server backfills that project, and when it is revoked it tells the device to purge it, so that data does not stay on the phone. A file is uploaded to blob storage separately, in chunks of about 5 MB with an upload session that reports how many bytes it holds, so a resumed upload continues from there. The mutation that attaches the file is queued behind the upload and refers to it by id, and the record shows the local copy until the upload finishes.
steps.tradeoff: Phones hold only their own data, and big uploads survive dropped connections and do not block small edits. Permission changes need their own events, partial copies make joins harder because a related record may not be on the device, and abandoned upload sessions need cleaning.

failures.scenario: The reply to a push is lost and the app sends the same batch again
failures.impact: Applied twice, a parts count of minus 3 would become minus 6, and a created checklist would appear twice.
failures.answer: Every mutation has a unique id. The server finds it among the ids it has applied, acknowledges it again and applies nothing. The client removes the rows from its outbox only when it sees the acknowledgement, so a lost reply causes a retry and never a loss.

failures.scenario: A phone with its clock 20 minutes fast edits a work order, and a colleague who has seen that edit changes the same field
failures.impact: With plain wall-clock timestamps the colleague's later, informed edit looks older and is discarded.
failures.answer: Timestamps come from a hybrid logical clock, so the colleague's edit is stamped after the change they saw. The server also refuses timestamps far in the future, for example more than a day ahead, because a wildly fast clock would otherwise win every conflict from then on.

failures.scenario: A phone comes back after 45 days offline
failures.impact: The tombstones it needs were collected, so incremental pulls cannot tell it which rows were deleted, and its old copy would show ghosts.
failures.answer: Its cursor is below the server's floor, so the server answers with a reset. The app pushes its outbox first, then replaces the local replica with a fresh snapshot of the data it may see, and carries on from the new cursor. Edits that touch records collected in the meantime go to the review queue.

failures.scenario: An app update changes the local schema while the outbox still holds unsent mutations in the old shape
failures.impact: If the migration drops or reshapes them, the user's offline work vanishes, and if the server rejects them, the whole outbox is stuck.
failures.answer: The migration rewrites the outbox rows together with the tables, inside one transaction, and each mutation carries a schema version. The server accepts older versions for a stated period and upgrades them on arrival. A single mutation that is invalid is moved aside and shown to the user, so it does not block the others.

failures.scenario: A technician is removed from a project while offline, then reconnects with edits to it
failures.impact: Their edits should not be accepted, yet the unsent batch also holds valid edits to other projects.
failures.answer: The server checks permission for each mutation and rejects only the ones for the project, with a reason. The client moves those rows to a rejected list that the user can see, keeps going with the rest of the batch, and on the next pull purges the project's data from the device.

alternatives.title: How to resolve conflicts

options.name: Whole record, last writer wins
options.pro: Trivial to build and to explain
options.con: A later save silently wipes out unrelated edits to other fields

options.name: Per field with a hybrid clock, counters and sets for mergeable values
options.pro: Most concurrent edits merge without anyone noticing
options.con: Metadata on every field, and two blind edits to one plain field still lose one

options.name: A full CRDT or operational transformation for the data
options.pro: Merges everything by construction, including text
options.con: Heavy for ordinary records, and history grows and needs compaction

options.name: Detect and ask the user
options.con: Interrupts the user, and nobody may be there to answer

alternatives.pick: Per-field merge with counters and sets, a review queue for a few fields where losing an edit is unacceptable, and a CRDT only for collaborative text.

alternatives.title: How clients ask for changes

options.name: A timestamp, 'changed since'
options.pro: Needs no extra column or log
options.con: Misses rows when commits are out of order or clocks differ

options.name: A sequence number from a change log
options.pro: Exact, resumable, and cheap to query with an index
options.con: The log must be kept and the counter written in order

options.name: A version vector per device
options.pro: Works with no central order, for peer-to-peer sync
options.con: Grows with the number of devices and is complex for a server-centred app

alternatives.pick: A sequence number from a change log per collection, since a server sits in the middle.

alternatives.title: How long to keep tombstones

options.name: For ever
options.pro: Any device can come back at any time
options.con: Storage and sync cost grow without limit

options.name: A fixed window, then a reset for old devices
options.pro: Bounded cost, and a simple rule to explain
options.con: A returning device pays for a full download

options.name: Until every known device has acknowledged
options.pro: Collects as early as it is safe
options.con: One dead phone blocks cleanup, unless devices are expired too

alternatives.pick: A fixed window a little longer than the offline promise, plus a reset, with devices unseen for longer than that removed from the registry.

alternatives.title: How the app learns that something changed

options.name: Poll every N seconds
options.con: Idle devices cost requests, and changes arrive up to N seconds late

options.name: A push hint, then pull
options.pro: Few requests, and the pull path is the only path for data
options.con: Needs a connection or push service, and a hint can be lost so a slow poll remains

options.name: Send the data itself over a socket
options.con: Two paths to keep consistent, and a missed message means a gap

alternatives.pick: A push hint followed by a pull, with a slow poll as a safety net.

roles.label: The app
roles.description: The phone or tablet app that the user taps.

roles.label: Sync entry point
roles.description: The sync API that devices push to and pull from.

roles.label: Outbox and review
roles.description: Unsent changes on the device and conflicts waiting for a person.

roles.label: Merge and cleanup
roles.description: Conflict rules, access filtering and tombstone collection.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The local database, server records, change log and blob storage.

quiz.question: A field app saves a parts change of minus 3 with a request to the server. On a weak connection the request times out after 10 seconds, and the app retries. Sometimes the first request had already been applied, and stock drops by 6. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the request timeout to 60 seconds, so replies get back before the client gives up and a retry is rarely needed
Stop retrying automatically and show an error, so the technician can check the order and save the change again later
Queue each change in an outbox with a unique id, and have the server acknowledge a repeated id without applying it
Send the new stock total instead of the change, so that applying the same request twice leaves the same number in place
quiz.explanation: A unique id lets the server tell a retry from a new change, so the retry is safe however many times it arrives. A longer timeout only makes the lost-reply case rarer, and it still happens when the signal drops. Sending the total is repeatable, but it overwrites a colleague's change to the same count.

quiz.question: An app promises that a phone can stay offline for 30 days. To save space, the server deletes tombstones 14 days after a delete and keeps a plain incremental pull for everyone. A phone returns after 20 days. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: The phone never hears that some rows were deleted and keeps ghost rows that it may send back. Keep tombstones past 30 days, and reset devices whose cursor is below the cleanup floor.
The phone downloads the entire change log again and takes much longer to sync, though the result is correct. Raise the page size so that the catch-up finishes faster and uses fewer requests.
The server rejects the phone's queued edits because their mutation ids have expired. Give every mutation a new id when the phone reconnects after a long absence.
The cursor numbers have restarted on the server, so the phone sees changes it already has. Store a timestamp with each cursor, so that old values are ignored.
quiz.explanation: Once a tombstone is gone, an incremental pull cannot say that a row was deleted, so a stale phone keeps it and can resurrect it. The retention window must be longer than the offline promise, and a client past the floor must start again from a snapshot. The other symptoms are invented: pulls only return later changes, and sequence numbers do not restart.

quiz.question: Stock for a part is one field, merged with last-writer-wins and a hybrid logical clock. The count is 40. Two inspectors take 5 and 3 parts while offline, then sync. The app shows 35 or 37 depending on who wrote last, but the real stock is 32. What is the best change?
options: Use more accurate device clocks, such as GPS time, so the server reliably picks the truly latest of the two writes
Store stock as per-device increments and sum them on merge, so both withdrawals count in any order
Detect the conflict and ask the second inspector to choose between 35 and 37, since a person knows the right number
Move to whole-record last-writer-wins, so one device's complete copy of the part always replaces the other's
quiz.explanation: Both withdrawals are valid and neither written total is right, so no clock can choose correctly. A counter that adds each device's changes gives 32. Asking the user is no help when neither candidate is right, and whole-record overwriting also drops one change.
